title: Why Fusionism Failed
author: Geoff Shullenberger
content:
![Why Fusionism
Failed](https://storage.ghost.io/c/65/af/65afbdb5-30bf-4286-acc4-9535069adb42/content/images/2026/09/YoungFSM2.jpg)

> _Fusionism: Liberty, Virtue, and the Future of the American Right_  
>  By Stephanie Slade  
> Notre Dame, 291 pages, $30

For centuries, conservative thinkers have asked themselves: Where did it all
go wrong? A few of them have settled on impersonal historical transitions like
the agricultural or industrial revolutions, but most answers have tended to
involve wrong turns in thought: the Gnostics, William of Ockham, Machiavelli.
As Richard Weaver put it in the title of his 1948 book (the locus classicus of
the "blame Ockham" narrative): _Ideas Have Consequences_. Among other
advantages, this approach assigns a heroic role to the conservative
intellectual, whose intervention might well prove capable of righting the
course of history once again.

Stephanie Slade's _Fusionism: Liberty, Virtue, and the Future of the American
Right_ is a new entry in this genre that also examines the careers of several
earlier practitioners, Weaver among them. For Slade, our current malaise dates
to a relatively recent fall from grace: the political rise of Donald Trump and
the seduction of the American right by ideologies associated with his MAGA
movement. Her concern is less with how nefarious ideas have gained traction--
she seems to regard MAGA-aligned intellectuals as opportunists rather than
substantive thinkers--than with how what she regards as a beneficent idea was
abandoned by her fellow conservatives. That idea is "fusionism," the
brainchild of Frank Meyer, the ex-communist, _National Review_ editor, and co-
founder of the American Conservative Union.

Meyer's core idea, Slade writes, was the "fusion of liberty and virtue."
Fusionists, she says, hold that "questions about the pursuit of virtue … ought
to be decided by individuals and families" and "ought _not_ be decided by the
state, which in a well-functioning society has the narrower mandate of
protecting basic rights and liberties." MAGA and its fellow travelers, she
believes, have fatally strayed from both precepts, disdaining virtue--for one
thing, by elevating a man so obviously lacking in it--and at the same time
pursuing the aggressive deployment of state power to achieve their ends.

For Slade, it is important that fusionism be understood as "a philosophical
synthesis, not a political alliance." The latter understanding is often cited
as grounds for dismissing it as outmoded: an ideological artifact of the Cold
War era, when free marketeers, religious conservatives, and hawkish
anticommunists made common cause to defeat the Red Menace. _Fusionism_ aims to
show that the titular worldview is no mere strategic alliance, but an
enduringly true normative account of human affairs.

By Slade's account, fusionism possesses a cohesiveness its would-be successors
lack. The groups she calls "theocons," "natcons," and "neoreactionaries" all
define themselves against fusionism to varyingly explicit degrees, but as she
notes, their objections are often at odds with each other: Some on the MAGA
right lament that the fusionist right failed to "use … government force to
create a more virtuous world," even as others are openly contemptuous of
Christian morality, whether in theory (Bronze Age Pervert's neopaganism) or
practice (Trump's own general impiety). In terms of Slade's core dichotomy,
while elites often seem drawn to Trumpism as a vehicle for the authoritarian
imposition of virtue, many voters seem to appreciate its libertarian--and
libertine--bent. Hence, paradoxically, right-wing intellectuals began to flirt
with ideas like making divorce illegal even as the GOP base was becoming more
pro-gambling and pro-weed.

Slade is more honest than other Never Trump conservatives about the
contradictions and conflicts that plagued the conservative movement in earlier
eras. She discusses the illiberal views and authoritarian sympathies of many
of the leading figures of the _National Review_ era, including Meyer himself.
She quotes Richard Weaver writing enviously of the "discipline" enforced by
Soviet authorities, in contrast to the moral chaos of the democratic West.
But, she argues, under Meyer's influence Weaver became more skeptical of state
coercion. Something like this even happened, she claims, with a key Meyer
antagonist: William F. Buckley's Franco-admiring brother-in-law Brent Bozell,
who although never altogether comfortable with Meyer's libertarianism, focused
in operational terms on "voluntary cooperation through civil society
institutions" as a "consummate institution builder." Meyer's fusionist vision,
Slade says, eventually prevailed over its rivals and became coterminous with
American conservative ideals.

Returning to the original question, where did it all go wrong? After
fusionism's triumph, why did the GOP fall so precipitously to Trump? Never
Trumpers who remain loyal to fusionism have tended to answer in two ways. The
first is to claim that it didn't go wrong at all--that the displacement of an
older, more virtuous version of conservatism by the Trumpian heresy is
something like a historical accident: the result of misinformation, perhaps,
or other contingent factors. The second is to claim that "real fusionism has
never been tried," that it was undone by its compromises with big government,
rather than by flaws in its basic ideological framework.

To her credit, Slade offers a more nuanced picture of fusionism's shifting
fortunes. As an electoral project, she argues, it reached its zenith in the
presidency of Ronald Reagan, who praised Meyer as a "great thinker" early in
his first term. But she also shows that Reagan was less of a fusionist in
practice than many of his admirers and detractors believe. She highlights in
particular his failure to curb the growth of government spending, which led to
the massive ballooning of federal deficits. She also acknowledges this was a
concession to a reality many conservatives prefer not to face up to: Shrinking
government just isn't very popular.

> "Shrinking government just isn't very popular."

In this area, Slade reluctantly admits that Trump is less of a deviation in
practice from Reagan than it might seem. "In a few areas," she even concedes,
"Trump has arguably hewed to Reagan's campaign promises more faithfully than
Reagan did"--especially when it comes to cutting and defunding disfavored
government programs. At the same time, he has also "been a shameless
profligate" when it comes to spending--but something similar was true of
Reagan, as Slade admits. The difference, she seems to think, was that Reagan
and other earlier GOP leaders at least "made gestures … to the importance of
basic fiscal responsibility," whereas Trump doesn't.

Again, conservatives limited themselves to making "gestures" because such cuts
are perpetually unpopular. The fusionist view that shrinking, privatizing, or
eliminating Social Security, Medicare, and Medicaid would enhance the liberty
and virtue of the American citizenry makes little sense to most American
citizens. The reason for this is, in part, a measure of what might be seen as
fusionism's success. The expansion of personal, professional, and
entrepreneurial liberty in modern America has been very real. Yet the society
forged by this vastly expanded freedom is also afflicted by precarity and
vulnerability. Entitlements at least theoretically mitigate that condition,
offering an island of relative certainty. Fusionists may perpetually lament
this fact, but it is a stubborn one that Reagan acceded to--as, later, did
George W. Bush when he retreated from his widely reviled plan to privatize
Social Security. A decade later, Trump capitalized on this fact by bucking the
Republican party line on cutting entitlements. What Slade calls the "timeless
American idea" of fusionism seems incapable of responding to this political
reality.

When we turn to the newer issues facing the body politic, a similar inadequacy
emerges. The most dramatic case concerns artificial intelligence, which has
become one of the central issues in American politics. It is an interesting
and revealing fact that the "conservative" position on AI is radically
unsettled. The Trump administration has largely adopted an accelerationist
stance, and plenty of right-of-center thinkers can be found who will argue
that such an approach is in line with the longstanding principles Slade puts
under the heading of liberty: essentially, minimal state intervention in
economic activities. Yet as Gregory Conti has
[_argued_](https://www.compactmag.com/article/the-ai-apocalypse-is-already-
here/) [_several_](https://www.compactmag.com/article/big-techs-war-on-human-
achievement/) [_times_](https://www.compactmag.com/article/on-ai-bernie-is-
the-last-conservative/) in these pages, a conservative should regard the
laissez-faire approach as seriously flawed and possibly catastrophic when it
comes to AI. The reason for this is that the inventors of AI openly seek to
bring about a revolution more radical than any previous one in history, one in
which humanity is reduced to a state of dependency far more absolute and
abject than welfare dependency.

At one point, Slade mentions that the conservative sage Russell Kirk referred
to automobiles as "mechanical jacobins." She treats this as a sign of his
personal eccentricity, but Kirk was hinting at a serious point: Material and
technological forces, and not just ideas, have consequences. What should the
fusionist, who seeks to balance liberty and virtue, have to say about a
revolution carried out not by statist ideologues but by entrepreneurs in the
private sector? Like many conservatives, Slade tends to treat liberty as
something that can only be curtailed by governments; subjugation by privately
owned technological systems doesn't figure in her account. But judging by the
surging revolt against data centers and Flock cameras, many Americans take the
prospect of private coercion seriously. Until it can speak to this concern,
fusionism isn't likely to make a comeback.
